skill.title: SQL
skill.summary: NULL logic, joins, indexing and transactions in PostgreSQL.
skill.description: Write queries that return what you mean, choose indexes from access patterns, read query plans, and reason about concurrent transactions.

questions.title: Comparing with NULL
questions.prompt: The `users` table contains 40 rows where `deleted_at` is NULL. What does this query return?
questions.code: SELECT count(*) FROM users WHERE deleted_at = NULL;

options.text: NULL
A syntax error

questions.explanation: Any ordinary comparison with NULL yields NULL (unknown), not true, and `WHERE` keeps only rows where the condition is true. No rows pass, so `count(*)` returns 0. Use `deleted_at IS NULL`.
rubric: Explains that `= NULL` evaluates to NULL (unknown).
Explains that `WHERE` keeps only rows where the condition is true.
Uses `IS NULL` as the fix.
misconceptions: `count(*)` returns NULL when no rows match.

resources.title: PostgreSQL docs: Comparison functions and operators

questions.acceptance_criteria: Answers 0, explains that comparisons with NULL are unknown, and uses IS NULL.

questions.title: A LEFT JOIN that isn't
questions.prompt: The intent is to list every user, with their paid orders where they exist. What does this query actually do?
questions.code:
SELECT u.id, o.id AS order_id
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id
WHERE o.status = 'paid';

options.text: Returns every user, with NULL `order_id` for users without paid orders
Excludes users without paid orders, behaving like an inner join
Returns every user once, ignoring the status filter
Fails because `WHERE` cannot reference the right-hand table of a LEFT JOIN

questions.explanation: Unmatched users get NULL for every `o` column; `o.status = 'paid'` is then NULL and `WHERE` removes those rows. Move the condition into the join (`ON o.user_id = u.id AND o.status = 'paid'`) to keep all users.
rubric: Explains that unmatched rows carry NULLs for the right-hand table.
Explains that the `WHERE` filter discards those NULL rows.
Moves the predicate into the `ON` clause.
misconceptions: LEFT JOIN always returns every row from the left table regardless of WHERE.
Filters in ON and WHERE are equivalent for outer joins.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Explains the WHERE filter removes unmatched rows and moves the predicate into the ON clause.

questions.title: Column order in a composite index
questions.prompt: `orders` has a B-tree index on `(customer_id, created_at)` and many distinct customers. Which query is least able to use this index efficiently?

options.text: `WHERE customer_id = 42 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20`
`WHERE customer_id = 42 AND created_at > now() - interval '7 days'`
`WHERE created_at > now() - interval '1 day'`
`WHERE customer_id IN (1, 2, 3)`

questions.explanation: A composite B-tree is ordered by its first column, then by the second within each first-column value. Queries that constrain the leading column can seek directly; a filter on `created_at` alone has no single range to scan. (PostgreSQL 18's skip scan can help when the leading column has few distinct values, which is not the case here.) Add an index on `created_at` if that query matters.
rubric: Explains that composite B-tree indexes are ordered by the leading column first.
Identifies that filtering only on the second column cannot seek efficiently.
Recognises that option (a) also avoids a sort.
Proposes a separate index while noting write and storage costs.
misconceptions: A composite index serves any query that mentions one of its columns.
Column order in a composite index doesn't matter.

resources.title: PostgreSQL docs: Indexes and ORDER BY

questions.acceptance_criteria: Identifies the created_at-only query and explains leading-column ordering.

questions.title: The lost update
questions.prompt: Two requests run this logic concurrently for the same account and the final balance is sometimes wrong. Name the anomaly, explain why PostgreSQL's default isolation level allows it, and give two different fixes.
questions.hint: Both transactions can read the same starting balance before either writes.
questions.explanation: This is a lost update: both read 100 and each writes its own result, so one change disappears. Under READ COMMITTED each statement sees committed data, and nothing ties the earlier read to the later write. Fixes: do the arithmetic in one statement (`SET balance = balance - 30`), lock the row with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, use optimistic concurrency with a version column, or run at REPEATABLE READ/SERIALIZABLE and retry on serialization failures.
rubric: Names the lost update anomaly and walks through the interleaving.
Explains why READ COMMITTED does not prevent it.
Gives an atomic single-statement update as one fix.
Gives a locking (`FOR UPDATE`) or optimistic-concurrency fix as another.
Mentions stronger isolation levels require retry handling.
misconceptions: Wrapping statements in a transaction automatically prevents all concurrency anomalies.
Higher isolation levels need no application-side handling.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Names the lost update, explains why READ COMMITTED allows it, and gives two valid fixes.

questions.title: Why isn't my index used?
questions.prompt: `users` has 5 million rows and a B-tree index on `email`. This query is slow and `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` shows a sequential scan. Explain the most likely cause, how you would confirm it, how you would fix it, and at least two other reasons PostgreSQL might legitimately skip an index.
questions.code: SELECT * FROM users WHERE lower(email) = lower($1);
questions.hint: What exactly is stored in the index, and what does the query compare?
questions.explanation: The index stores `email`, but the query filters on `lower(email)`, an expression the index cannot answer. Create an expression index on `lower(email)` (or use a case-insensitive type such as `citext`), then confirm with `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)`. The planner may also skip an index when a predicate matches a large fraction of rows, when statistics are stale (`ANALYZE`), on type mismatches, or when the table is small.
rubric: Identifies that the index cannot serve a predicate on `lower(email)`.
Proposes an expression index on `lower(email)` or a case-insensitive type.
Describes confirming the fix with `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`.
Gives at least two other legitimate reasons, such as low selectivity or stale statistics.
Considers enforcing uniqueness on the normalised value.
misconceptions: PostgreSQL always uses an index if one exists on the column.
A sequential scan is always a sign of a bug.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Identifies the lower(email) mismatch, proposes an expression index, and names another legitimate reason for a sequential scan.

questions.title: Counting orders per user
questions.prompt: Ada has three orders and Grace has none. What does this query return for Grace?
questions.code:
SELECT u.name, count(*) AS orders
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id
GROUP BY u.name;
questions.hint: How many rows does the join produce for Grace before grouping?

options.text: `NULL`
No row at all for Grace

questions.explanation: The LEFT JOIN keeps Grace with NULLs for every `o` column, producing one row. `count(*)` counts rows, not orders, so Grace gets 1. `count(o.id)` counts only non-NULL values and returns 0 for her.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Selects “1”. The LEFT JOIN keeps Grace with NULLs for every `o` column, producing one row.
rubric: States that Grace gets 1.
Explains that the LEFT JOIN produces one row of NULLs.
Uses `count(o.id)` (a non-NULL column) to count matches.
misconceptions: A LEFT JOIN drops users without matches.

questions.title: Two doctors go off call
questions.prompt: At least one doctor must stay on call. Two on-call doctors run this transaction at the same moment under PostgreSQL's REPEATABLE READ. What can happen?
questions.hint: Do the two transactions update the same row?

options.text: Both commit, leaving nobody on call; SERIALIZABLE would abort one of them
The second transaction blocks until the first commits, then sees one doctor
One fails with a unique violation because both update the same table
Both commit, but PostgreSQL automatically re-runs the check afterwards

questions.explanation: Each transaction reads a snapshot showing two doctors on call, passes the check, and updates a different row. The writes do not conflict, so REPEATABLE READ (snapshot isolation) lets both commit: a write skew. SERIALIZABLE detects the dangerous read/write dependency and aborts one transaction with a serialization failure, which the application must retry. Alternatives are locking the rows read (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`) or modelling the rule as a constraint.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Selects “Both commit, leaving nobody on call; SERIALIZABLE would abort one of them”. Each transaction reads a snapshot showing two doctors on call, passes the check, and updates a different row.
rubric: Identifies write skew and the outcome (nobody on call).
Explains why snapshot isolation allows it (different rows updated).
States that SERIALIZABLE aborts one transaction and requires retries.
Mentions an alternative such as `FOR UPDATE` on the rows read.
misconceptions: REPEATABLE READ prevents all concurrency anomalies.
Transactions updating different rows can never conflict.

questions.title: Deep pages are slow
questions.prompt: A feed uses `ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET $offset` with an index on `created_at`. The first page takes 2 ms, but page 5,000 takes over a second. What is the best fix?
questions.hint: How many rows must the database step over to return page 5,000?

options.text: Add a second index on `created_at` in descending order for the feed
Keyset pagination: seek past the last row with `(created_at, id) < ($1, $2)`
Raise `work_mem` so the sort for each deep page fits in memory
Run `VACUUM FULL` so rows are physically stored in `created_at` order

questions.explanation: An index lets the database read rows in order, but OFFSET still has to walk past and discard every skipped row, so page 5,000 reads about 100,000 index entries. Keyset pagination remembers the last row seen and seeks straight to it, so every page costs the same. Including `id` as a tiebreaker keeps the order stable when timestamps repeat; an index on `(created_at, id)` supports it. The trade-off is no jumping to arbitrary page numbers.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Selects “Keyset pagination: seek past the last row with `(created_at, id) < ($1, $2)”. An index lets the database read rows in order, but OFFSET still has to walk past and discard every skipped row, so page 5,000 reads about 100,000 index entries.
rubric: Explains that OFFSET reads and discards the skipped rows.
Proposes keyset (seek) pagination using the last row's values.
Adds a unique tiebreaker for a stable order.
Mentions the trade-off of losing random page access.
misconceptions: An index makes any OFFSET fast.
Sorting is the slow part of deep pagination.
